title: Dune
author: Frank Herbert
movie: Dune: Part One and Dune: Part Two
description: A desert planet, an imperial transfer of power, and a young heir's uncertain future anchor Herbert's landmark political science-fiction novel.
whyRead: The novel gives more room to the ecological systems, competing institutions, and inner calculations behind the Atreides and Fremen. It makes a useful companion to the films' visual scale.
readingGuide: Read the novel first if you want the political and ecological texture; watch first if you prefer to meet the world through Villeneuve's visual interpretation.

title: The Martian
author: Andy Weir
description: An astronaut stranded on Mars turns survival into a sequence of engineering problems, experiments, and improvised plans.
whyRead: Weir's novel lets readers follow the calculations and setbacks at a granular pace, turning optimism into a repeatable method rather than a personality trait.
readingGuide: Read first for the problem-solving detail; watch first for a brisk, character-centered survival adventure.

title: Jurassic Park
author: Michael Crichton
description: A showcase theme park built around cloned dinosaurs becomes a stress test for systems that were designed to impress investors before they were ready for reality.
whyRead: Crichton's thriller gives more space to chaos theory, corporate incentives, and the gap between a system that works in a demo and one that survives failure.
readingGuide: Watch first for Spielberg's suspenseful adventure; read first if you want a denser techno-thriller and more systems-level detail.

title: The Lord of the Rings
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
movie: The Lord of the Rings film trilogy (2001–2003)
description: A small fellowship carries a dangerous object across a vast world while resisting the promise that power can be used safely by the right person.
whyRead: Tolkien's prose deepens the landscapes, histories, songs, and quiet acts of endurance that make the journey feel larger than its battles.
readingGuide: Read first to travel through Tolkien's language and history; watch first for a clear cinematic path into the fellowship and its world.

title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
author: Philip K. Dick
relationship: Inspired the original Blade Runner; not a direct adaptation of Blade Runner 2049
description: A bounty hunter's assignment to identify androids becomes an unsettling inquiry into empathy, artificial life, and the categories humans use to protect their status.
whyRead: Dick's novel is shorter and stranger than the films, with its own world and questions. Reading it clarifies the source of the premise without implying the screen stories are interchangeable.
readingGuide: Read first for the novel's distinct take on empathy; watch first if you want to encounter each film as its own interpretation.

title: Story of Your Life
author: Ted Chiang
description: A linguist's work with an unfamiliar language opens a story about communication, memory, and the shape of a life.
whyRead: Chiang's novella offers a compact, precise companion to Arrival and makes the relationship between language and perception feel intimate rather than merely theoretical.
readingGuide: Read first for the original short story's quiet structure; watch first to experience how Villeneuve translates its ideas into image and sound.
